chapter_title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read (How I Taught My Grandmother to Read)
subject: English
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 50 minutes × 8 periods = 400 minutes
Total: 8 periods · 6h 40min

periods.section_title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read
periods.activity_title: Activating Prior Knowledge and Entering the Story

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Reflect and Respond (p.1): word web — why reading and writing matter
Reflect and Respond (p.1): four oral-share questions on elderly relatives and shared experiences

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the chapter title and invites students to consider what it means to be illiterate in a literate household. Students complete the word web individually, jotting reasons why reading and writing matter in their own lives.

Teacher reads the story aloud from p.1 to p.6, students following in their textbooks; teacher pauses briefly at key moments — the grandmother listening to Kashi Yatre, the delayed magazine — to allow students to absorb the village setting and Krishtakka's character.

Class discussion using the four oral-share questions from Reflect and Respond: which languages elderly relatives speak, how time is shared with them, favourite experiences, and something the elderly enjoy watching young people do. Students share in pairs first, then with the class.

Teacher draws together the strands of discussion, connecting students' real experiences of elderly relatives to the grandmother Krishtakka's world; students note two or three key ideas about the story's setting in their exercise books.

periods.teacher_notes: The word web and oral questions work best when students draw on personal experience first — the grandmother Krishtakka's dependence on the narrator mirrors the dependency students may have noticed in their own families. Watch for students who conflate illiteracy with low intelligence; use the prose summary's detail that Krishtakka discusses Kashi Yatre intelligently at the temple courtyard to counter that assumption early.

periods.section_title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read
periods.activity_title: Cause, Effect and the Midnight Turning Point

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Reading for Meaning (p.2): match eight highlighted words to their meanings
Check Your Understanding (p.6–7): cause-and-effect table based on Part I of the story

homework.task_brief: Check Your Understanding (p.6): written response — did narrator expect grandmother in tears?

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the passage in the textbook at p.2 aloud; students follow and underline the eight highlighted words — protagonist, debate, episode, community, concentration, eagerly, convincing, guided — as they encounter them in context.

Students work in pairs to match the eight words to their meanings from the box; pairs share answers and teacher confirms, drawing attention to how context clues in the passage make several matches accessible without a dictionary.

Teacher reads aloud the section of the story covering Part I (up to the grandmother's tears and the midnight terrace scene, p.6–7); students then complete the cause-and-effect table in pairs, filling all six rows and sharing with the class.

Whole-class discussion on the effect rows: why Krishtakka felt too ashamed to ask a neighbour for help, and what the midnight terrace conversation reveals about the grandmother's inner life; teacher helps students articulate the distinction between financial comfort and dignified independence.

periods.teacher_notes: The cause-and-effect table has six rows and students sometimes conflate cause and effect in the first and fifth rows — both concern the grandmother never having gone to school. Use the prose summary detail that Krishtakka stoically faced life's hardships yet wept over a missed magazine episode to show students that the shame of helplessness, not grief, is the cause here. The homework question on expectations can be set as a brief written reflection.

periods.section_title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read
periods.activity_title: Critical Reflection on Resolution and Character

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Critical Reflection (p.10–11): true-or-false statements on Part II of the story
Critical Reflection (p.10–12): Extract 1 — five close-reading sub-questions on the terrace scene

homework.task_brief: Check Your Understanding (p.6): written response — how might narrator help grandmother learn?

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads aloud the resolution section of the story — Krishtakka's declaration, the Dassara deadline, the tuition, and the foot-touching ceremony — from p.9–12, students following; teacher pauses at the line 'For a good cause if you are determined, you can overcome any obstacle' and invites immediate student reactions.

Students work individually on the six true-or-false statements about Part II, then compare answers in pairs; teacher leads a quick whole-class check, asking students to cite the exact lines that confirm or refute each statement.

Class reads Extract 1 (the terrace scene, p.10–11) together; teacher guides close reading through all five sub-questions — the phrase 'never seen her cry', the choice of 'emotional', the rural-setting clue, the lines establishing tenderness, and the aspect not emphasised — students write brief answers and discuss in pairs before sharing.

Teacher draws together the session by asking: what does the extract reveal about how Sudha Murty uses atmosphere to carry the story's emotional weight? Students articulate one observation each in a round.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often mark the statement about the grandmother asking a neighbour for help as true; the prose summary is explicit that she felt too ashamed to ask — use this to discuss pride and the social dimension of illiteracy. Extract 1's sub-question on the rural-setting clue typically elicits the detail of the open terrace and the midnight conversation, which are strong anchors for the atmosphere question that follows.

periods.section_title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read
periods.activity_title: Deep Analysis — Extract 2 and Extended Response

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Critical Reflection (p.12): Extract 2 — five close-reading sub-questions on grandmother's declaration
Critical Reflection (p.12–13): seven extended-answer questions on theme, character and title

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly recaps the terrace scene and Krishtakka's declaration examined in the previous work on Extract 1, then introduces Extract 2 — Krishtakka's statement 'I want to be independent' and the narrator's childish mockery — as the pivot of the story's second movement.

Students read Extract 2 (p.12) individually, then work through all five sub-questions in pairs: Krishtakka's desire for self-sufficiency, the age-limit fill-in, the narrator's reason for laughing, two qualities of the grandmother, and how the narrator makes assumptions; pairs share and teacher confirms with class.

Teacher assigns the seven extended-answer questions (p.12–13) in a structured writing task: students choose three questions to answer in full paragraphs, ensuring at least one question addresses the foot-touching ceremony and at least one addresses the broader theme of the story; students draft their responses.
Two or three students share one extended response each; class offers brief oral feedback focusing on whether the response names specific textual evidence from the story.

periods.teacher_notes: The seven extended-answer questions are the analytical core of the chapter; budgeting all seven in full would overrun the available time, so guiding students to choose three ensures quality over quantity. Watch for students who treat the grandmother's foot-touching merely as politeness — the prose summary is explicit that Krishtakka is honouring her teacher, not her granddaughter, which is the story's moral inversion.

periods.section_title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read
periods.activity_title: Binomials, Prefixes, Idioms and Tense in Context

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.13): match eight binomials to meanings, then use five in sentences
Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.14): add negative prefixes to ten words
Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.15): match six learning-related idioms to meanings

homework.task_brief: Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.14): identify five words with prefixes from the story and write sentences

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the concept of binomials using 'hide and seek' from the story, explaining the fixed-order convention; students match all eight binomials (Column 1) to their meanings (Column 2) using dictionary support where needed, then write five of them in original sentences themed around Krishtakka's world.

Teacher explains negative-meaning prefixes using examples from the story (unhappy, unusual, independent, irrespective); students add the correct prefix from the box to each of the ten words in Column 1 and check answers in pairs.

Teacher introduces the six learning-related idioms using 'passed with flying colours' from the story as the entry point; students match idioms to meanings individually, then the class discusses which idioms best describe Krishtakka's learning journey and why.
Quick whole-class review: teacher reads an idiom aloud and students use it in a spoken sentence about the story's characters; teacher confirms usage and notes common errors for future practice.

periods.teacher_notes: Binomials and idioms should be anchored to the story's language throughout — asking students which idioms describe Krishtakka's effort ('burn the midnight oil', 'learn by heart') keeps the vocabulary work connected to comprehension. The prefix task is straightforward for most students but 'disrespect' and 'misunderstand' sometimes attract the wrong prefix — allow dictionary use and encourage peer checking.

periods.section_title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read
periods.activity_title: Digital Literacy Listening and Turncoat Debate

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Listen and Respond (p.17): complete five sentence-blanks from a talk on digital literacy
Speaking Activity (p.17): turncoat solo debate — two topics, one minute for and one minute against each

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly connects digital literacy to the story's theme: Krishtakka was cut off from her serial novel; today's equivalent gap is digital illiteracy. Teacher distributes or displays the five incomplete sentences from the textbook and reads the listening task instructions.

Teacher reads the digital literacy transcript aloud (p.259) at a clear, steady pace; students listen and complete the five blanks with one to three exact words. Teacher reads the transcript a second time, allowing students to check and fill any remaining blanks.

Class checks the five answers together; teacher draws attention to how the transcript defines digital literacy expansively — accessing, creating and sharing information — and links this to the DISHA/NDLM scheme, inviting one or two brief student observations.

Turncoat debate: teacher explains the format (one minute for, one minute against, same speaker). Two or three volunteers take Topic 2 ('Learning can happen only when you are young'); remaining students take Topic 1 in pairs simultaneously, then two pairs share their strongest arguments with the class. Teacher gives brief feedback on reasoning clarity and argument structure.

periods.teacher_notes: The listening transcript connects naturally to the chapter's literacy theme — digital literacy is the contemporary parallel to Krishtakka's print literacy; use this connection explicitly when checking the blanks. For the turncoat debate, students often find the 'against' side of Topic 2 easier because the story itself disproves it — encourage them to make the 'for' argument genuinely rather than perfunctorily.

periods.section_title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read
periods.activity_title: Letter to the Editor — Planning, Drafting and Revising

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Writing Task (p.17): formal letter to editor on student participation in adult literacy camps

time_bands.activity: Teacher recaps formal letter format using the textbook's 'Points to Remember' guidance: sender details, date, subject line of four to five words, salutation, three-paragraph body, and 'Yours truly' close. Teacher models a brief subject line and opening sentence on the board, highlighting register and specificity.

Students plan their letter: individually they list three arguments (importance of student participation, benefits for students and society, ways to spread awareness) and note one concrete example or statistic for each argument; teacher circulates and prompts students whose plans are too general.

Students draft the complete letter in their exercise books, applying the formal letter format and working through all three body paragraphs; teacher circulates, offering brief formative feedback on paragraph focus and language register.

Peer revision: students swap letters with a partner and check one element each — format completeness, formal register, and whether the letter makes a specific suggestion for spreading awareness. Partners annotate briefly before returning.

Students make one or two targeted revisions based on peer feedback; teacher invites one student to read their letter's subject line and opening sentence aloud, and the class evaluates its clarity and formality.

periods.teacher_notes: The most common weakness in this letter is the third paragraph — students often repeat the importance argument rather than suggesting concrete awareness strategies. Prompt students to think of specific actions (school volunteer drives, notice boards, social media posts) rather than abstract calls to action. Peer revision works best when each reviewer is assigned a single criterion rather than a general 'improve this'.

periods.section_title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read
periods.activity_title: Past Perfect in Context and Multilingual Kinship Exploration

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.16): simple past vs past perfect — fill in five sentences
Learning Beyond the Text (p.21): complete kinship-terms table across five Indian languages

homework.task_brief: Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.16): fill in ten blanks in the financial-planning paragraph using correct tense

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the simple past versus past perfect distinction using two sentences from the story — 'Secretly, I bought Kashi Yatre which had been published as a novel' and 'I knew that my student had passed with flying colours' — drawing the timeline on the board and asking students which action came first in each pair.

Students fill in the five sentences (A–E) on p.16, choosing simple past or past perfect for each blank; teacher circulates and then leads a whole-class check, asking students to explain their tense choices by naming the earlier and later events.

Teacher introduces the multilingual kinship table using the example already in the textbook — 'Avva' for grandmother in north Karnataka Kannada — and asks students to pool their knowledge to fill in six kinship terms across five Indian languages; students work in small groups, consulting classmates who speak different languages and referring to the textbook guidance on p.21.

Groups share their completed tables briefly; teacher highlights patterns across language families and connects the multilingual work back to the story's setting in Karnataka, noting how the word 'Avva' carries the story's emotional warmth.

periods.teacher_notes: The tense exercise works best when students draw an event-sequence diagram before filling in the blanks — sentence A (the delegates arriving after the keynote had begun) is the clearest model. For the kinship table, classes with students from diverse linguistic backgrounds will naturally produce richer data; where diversity is limited, encourage students to research at home and treat the table as a starting point rather than a complete product.

items.source_section_title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read
items.source_lo: Student analyses character motivation, authorial purpose, and theme by close-reading a prose narrative.
items.source_context: Krishtakka's decision to learn to read at sixty-two, her shame at dependence, and the symbolic foot-touching ceremony.
items.item_stem: When the narrator returned from the wedding, she found Krishtakka weeping — something she had never witnessed before, even through life's hardships. Which of the following best explains why Krishtakka was in tears?

options.label: A
options.text: She was grieving over a personal loss that had occurred while the narrator was away.

options.label: B
options.text: She felt helpless and ashamed because she could not read the new magazine episode on her own.

options.label: C
options.text: She was angry that the narrator had stayed away for longer than expected without informing her.

options.label: D
options.text: She was upset because the weekly Karmaveera magazine had not arrived while the narrator was gone.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Confuses Krishtakka's emotional state with grief; misses that the source is shame at illiteracy, not bereavement.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Misreads the emotional cause as anger at the narrator's absence rather than shame at her own dependence.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Partially correct about the magazine but misses that the magazine did arrive — Krishtakka simply could not read it herself.

items.source_section_title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read
items.source_lo: Student analyses character motivation, authorial purpose, and theme by close-reading a prose narrative.
items.source_context: Krishtakka's decision to learn to read at sixty-two, her shame at dependence, and the symbolic foot-touching ceremony.
items.item_stem:
Read the following extract from the story and answer the questions below.

1. What does Krishtakka's decision to set the Saraswati Puja day as her learning deadline reveal about her character? Refer to at least one specific detail from the extract.
2. The narrator initially laughs at Krishtakka's plan. How does Sudha Murty use this contrast between the narrator's reaction and Krishtakka's quiet dignity to develop the story's theme?
3. At the close of the story, Krishtakka touches the narrator's feet. Analyse what this gesture communicates about the relationship between age, learning, and respect, and explain how it reframes the story's central theme.
items.visual_stimulus: Krishtakka said she had decided she wanted to learn the Kannada alphabet and set Saraswati Puja day during Dassara as her deadline. The narrator laughed childishly at the old lady. But she just smiled. Tuition began the next morning. Krishtakka proved to be a diligent student — she read, repeated, wrote, and recited. By the Dassara festival she met her deadline. In a deeply symbolic gesture, she touched the narrator's feet, explaining that she was honouring not her granddaughter but her teacher.

expected_elements: Q1: Identifies determination and purposeful self-discipline through the Dassara deadline.
Q2: Notes the narrator's mockery contrasts with Krishtakka's calm, deepening the theme of late-life learning.
Q2: Recognises Murty uses the contrast to critique assumptions about age and ability.
Q3: Explains the foot-touching reverses the elder–younger hierarchy, honouring the teacher not the granddaughter.
Q3: Links gesture to the theme that learning dissolves social hierarchy and age barriers.

items.source_section_title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read
items.source_lo: Student listens to an informational talk and retrieves specific details by completing sentence-level blanks.
items.source_context: A speaker's talk defining digital literacy and its three benefits, including the DISHA/NDLM scheme.
items.item_stem:
Listen to the talk on digital literacy. Complete the following sentences with the exact words heard in the talk.
(A) According to the speaker, digital literacy means accessing, creating, and sharing information using ____________.
(B) One of digital literacy's key benefits is that it helps senior citizens to ____________.
(C) The programme formulated to impart IT training across the country is called the Digital Saksharta Abhiyan, also known as the ____________.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: (A) technology. (B) stay connected. (C) National Digital Literacy Mission (NDLM) Scheme.

items.source_section_title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read
items.source_lo: Student listens to an informational talk and retrieves specific details by completing sentence-level blanks.
items.source_context: A speaker's talk defining digital literacy and its three benefits, including the DISHA/NDLM scheme.
items.item_stem: The speaker in the digital literacy talk says that safe internet use involves recognising 'misinformation, scams, and cyber threats.' In two to three sentences, explain what you understand by 'misinformation' in the context of this talk, and suggest one practical step a student could take to protect themselves from it.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Misinformation refers to false or inaccurate information that circulates online, which the speaker identifies as one of the risks that digital literacy helps people recognise. A practical step a student could take is to verify information by checking a second reliable source before sharing it.

items.source_lo: Student argues for and against a proposition with reasons, switching sides within a solo debate format.
items.source_context: Turncoat debate on whether learning can happen only when young, drawing on the story's theme.
items.item_stem: Describe a specific moment from the story of Krishtakka that you would use as evidence if you were arguing FOR the statement 'It is never too late to learn.' Speak for up to one minute, naming the moment and explaining why it supports the argument.

expected_elements: Names a specific moment — Krishtakka's Dassara deadline or the foot-touching ceremony.
Explains clearly why the moment supports the 'never too late' argument.
Uses at least one reason grounded in Krishtakka's determination or diligence.
Speaks in coherent sentences with a clear beginning and a closing statement.

items.source_section_title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read
items.source_lo: Student argues for and against a proposition with reasons, switching sides within a solo debate format.
items.source_context: Turncoat debate on whether learning can happen only when young, drawing on the story's theme.
items.item_stem: Using the turncoat format, argue BOTH sides of the following proposition — speaking for no more than one minute on each side: 'Literacy in one's mother tongue is more important than digital literacy in today's world.' Begin by arguing FOR the proposition, then switch and argue AGAINST it. You may draw on the story of Krishtakka or on examples from your own experience.

expected_elements: FOR side: presents at least one reasoned argument for mother-tongue literacy's primacy.
AGAINST side: presents at least one reasoned argument for digital literacy's importance.
Each side is supported with a reason or example, not assertion alone.
Speaker switches sides clearly and maintains the turncoat format.
Arguments demonstrate engagement with both the story's context and contemporary relevance.

items.source_section_title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read
items.source_lo: Student writes a formal letter to an editor making a structured argument with evidence and a call to action.
items.source_context: A community campaign to bring free reading materials to rural senior citizens' centres.
items.item_stem: Write a short notice (80–100 words) for your school notice board, informing students about an upcoming awareness rally on the importance of mother-tongue literacy for senior citizens in rural areas. Include the date, venue, organising body, and a clear call to participate. Use formal language and an appropriate notice format.

expected_elements: Notice format observed: heading, date, venue, organising body present.
Purpose and call to action are clearly and specifically stated.
Language is formal and appropriate to the notice genre.
Content connects to the theme of mother-tongue or senior-citizen literacy.

items.source_section_title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read
items.source_lo: Student writes a formal letter to an editor making a structured argument with evidence and a call to action.
items.source_context: A community campaign to bring free reading materials to rural senior citizens' centres.
items.item_stem: Write a letter to the Editor of a regional newspaper arguing that public libraries in rural areas should extend their evening hours and stock reading material in regional languages, so that working adults and senior citizens have access to print literacy resources. Your letter should be 150–200 words, use formal letter format, and include at least one specific suggestion and one benefit for the community.

expected_elements: Formal letter format followed: sender details, date, subject line, salutation, close.
Argument is clearly stated and supported with at least one specific reason.
At least one concrete suggestion for the library's extended service is included.
A community benefit — for working adults or senior citizens — is explicitly identified.
Language is formal, register consistent throughout, and within the word-count range.

items.source_lo: Student identifies and applies binomials, negative prefixes, idiomatic expressions, and simple past versus past perfect tense in context.
items.source_context: Binomials and learning-related idioms from the story's language; simple past and past perfect in narrative sentences.
items.item_stem:
The narrator says: 'I knew, then, that my student had passed with flying colours.' Rewrite the following three sentences so that each correctly uses either the simple past or the past perfect tense to show the sequence of events. Write the complete sentence for each.
(i) By the time Krishtakka (receive) the copy of Kashi Yatre, she (already learn) to read the Kannada alphabet.
(ii) The narrator (return) from the wedding before she (realise) how much her grandmother had suffered.
(iii) When Krishtakka (touch) the narrator's feet, the narrator (understand) the true meaning of the gesture.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: (i) By the time Krishtakka received the copy of Kashi Yatre, she had already learned to read the Kannada alphabet. (ii) The narrator returned from the wedding before she realised how much her grandmother had suffered. (iii) When Krishtakka touched the narrator's feet, the narrator understood the true meaning of the gesture.

items.item_stem: The story tells us that in north Karnataka, the word 'Avva' means grandmother. Name the word for grandmother in any three Indian languages other than Kannada and English. Write one sentence for each word explaining which language it belongs to.

expected_elements: Three distinct Indian languages named — not Kannada or English.
Correct or plausible kinship term for grandmother given for each language.
Each term is placed in a clear sentence naming its language.
Response shows awareness of linguistic diversity within India.

items.source_section_title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read
items.source_lo: Student explores linguistic and cultural diversity by researching kinship terms across Indian languages.
items.source_context: Kinship vocabulary in five Indian languages, beginning with 'Avva' for grandmother in north Karnataka Kannada.
items.item_stem: Design a short multilingual project plan (100–120 words) for a classroom display titled 'Words That Connect Us.' Your plan should explain: (a) which five Indian languages you would feature and why, (b) which kinship terms you would display and what they tell us about family structures across cultures, and (c) how the display connects to the idea of literacy and cultural identity explored in the story of Krishtakka.

expected_elements: Five Indian languages named with a brief rationale for selection.
Specific kinship terms identified and their cultural significance explained.
Clear connection drawn between language diversity and cultural identity.
Explicit link made to the story's theme of literacy and belonging.
Plan is coherent, within word count, and written in an appropriate register.
